name: Androstadienone / copulins claims
lead: Androstadienone is a steroid found in human sweat, semen and other body secretions, and copulins are a group of volatile fatty acids found in vaginal fluid. Both have been proposed as human pheromones, meaning chemical signals that could change the mood, physiology or behavior of other people without conscious awareness.[1][2][3] A second compound often grouped with androstadienone is estratetraenol, an estrane steroid proposed as its counterpart in women.[21][17]

In appearance and attraction circles the appeal is straightforward: a scent that works below conscious notice would make the wearer more attractive without changing how they look. Androstadienone is sold as an additive in men's fragrances and body sprays on the premise that it raises sexual attraction, while copulins are discussed as a signal of female fertility.[1][2] Accordingly the topic sits alongside fragrance, hygiene and grooming as a way people try to improve the impression they make.

Laboratory studies have reported small effects of androstadienone on women's mood, attention to emotional information and cortisol levels, and brain-imaging studies have reported activation in regions related to social cognition.[1][10][16] Reviews state that no pheromonal substance has been shown in a peer-reviewed study to directly change human behavior and that the field is limited by small samples, publication bias and weak methods, while other researchers argue that humans may still have pheromones that have not yet been demonstrated.[2][5][6]

paras: Androstadienone (androsta-4,16-dien-3-one, often abbreviated AND) is a 16-androstene steroid made in the body from androstadienol by the enzyme 3-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase. It can be converted by 5-alpha-reductase into androstenone, which in turn can become androstenol. Although related to the androgen sex hormones, it has no androgenic or anabolic effects.[1][4] It is found in male sweat, saliva and semen and at much higher concentrations in men than in women.[15][16]

Estratetraenol (estra-1,3,5(10),16-tetraen-3-ol) is an estrane steroid related to estradiol that was first identified in the urine of pregnant women in 1968. Wikipedia reports that it is made from androstadienone by aromatase and has no known estrogenic effects; it is the compound most often paired with androstadienone as a candidate female-linked chemosignal.[21]

Copulins are six short-chain fatty acids, with acetic acid among them, first described in the vaginal fluid of rhesus monkeys. In women, about a third have all six, and levels rise before ovulation. Because human ovulation is concealed, their function in people is unclear and may not be sexual.[3]

The word pheromone was introduced in 1959 by Peter Karlson and Martin Luscher, building on work such as Adolf Butenandt's identification of the silkworm attractant bombykol in 1961.[2][3] Androstenone was the first mammalian pheromone identified, in boar saliva, where it triggers a mating stance in sows and has been sold to farmers for timing artificial insemination.[4]

Human research followed, focusing on underarm steroids, vaginal acids and the vomeronasal organ. In 1971 Martha McClintock reported menstrual synchrony in women, a finding later questioned on methodological grounds by Strassmann (1999) and Yang and Schank (2006). In 1978 Kirk-Smith reported that androstenol led people wearing treated masks to rate photographs as warmer and friendlier, in 1983 Van Toller and colleagues measured skin conductance responses to androstenone, and in 1998 Stern and McClintock reported that human body-odor compounds could regulate ovulation timing.[2][3]

Brain-imaging work added a further strand. Savic and colleagues (2001) reported sex-differentiated hypothalamic activation in response to androstadienone and estratetraenol, and later studies by Berglund and colleagues (2006, 2008) examined responses in lesbian women and male-to-female transsexual people. A 2021 review of this literature described the two steroids as candidate human sex pheromones that, in some studies, produce sexually dimorphic effects on perception, mood and arousal and different hypothalamic responses depending on the recipient's sex and sexual orientation.[21][17]

In most terrestrial mammals pheromones are detected by the vomeronasal organ or the olfactory epithelium and relayed to the amygdala and hypothalamus.[17] In humans the vomeronasal organ appears in the fetus but is atrophied or absent in adults, and its receptor genes are nonfunctional pseudogenes, so a 2013 review notes that adults have no functioning organ of this kind and that any detection would occur through the ordinary olfactory system.[2][16]

Proponents point to trace amine-associated receptors, identified in the mouse olfactory epithelium in 2006 and present in human form, as a candidate detector, and note that people can smell androstadienone although sensitivity varies widely from person to person.[2][16] A 2011 review observed that the compound's physiological levels in sweat appear too low to produce a response under experimental conditions, and that many researchers prefer to consider whole axillary extracts, a kind of mixture whose active components are still unidentified, rather than a single molecule; it also raised the possibility that androstadienone acts at low concentrations depending on context.[14] A 2023 study of older U.S. adults reported that individual sensitivity to androstadienone was associated with attention to emotions, social interactions and sexual behavior.[20]

Grosser and colleagues (2000) reported that very small amounts of androstadienone reduced nervousness and negative feelings in women. Lundstrom and Olsson (2005) found mood effects in heterosexual women that depended on whether a male or female experimenter was present, without any overt behavior change. Hummer and McClintock (2009) reported that the compound shifted attention toward emotional information, and Wyart and colleagues (2007) reported that smelling it altered women's cortisol.[1] A study of subthreshold exposure reported psychological effects in participants who could not consciously detect the compound.[19]

A 2013 review of studies in which women applied a pharmacological amount of androstadienone to the upper lip summarised improved mood and heightened focus on emotional information, and noted that some studies found benefits for sexual desire and arousal, though these depended on experimental context such as whether a male attendant was present.[16] A 2014 review stressed that effects differ by the recipient's sex and sexual orientation and by contextual conditions.[15]

Reviews note that the effects are mood or attention shifts rather than changes in mate choice, and that results are inconsistent between individuals and settings, with some studies finding no effect at all.[1][2]

A PET imaging study of five young women found that androstadienone activated a widely distributed network of brain regions related to social cognition compared with pleasant, unpleasant and neutral odours.[10] A later study in men reported that the compound increased individualistic behavior and decreased cooperative responses.[11] A 2020 randomized trial reported a rightward shift in women's preferences along the femininity-masculinity continuum of male faces, and a 2023 trial with 206 participants examined proactive and reactive aggression with sex-dependent results.[8][7] A 2026 randomized trial reported that androstadienone reduced women's mate-choice copying, with the effect moderated by intrasexual competition.[18]

A pre-registered 2024 study in Royal Society Open Science reported little evidence that androstadienone affects social-distance-dependent prosocial behaviour.[9] A 2025 review in Physiology & Behavior concluded that classifying androstadienone as a human sex pheromone remains inconclusive and called for methodological standardization.[5] A 2020 review in Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B noted that almost 60 studies have claimed significant results for putative human pheromones, that these may include false positives, and that pre-registration and Registered Reports are needed; it added that humans may still have pheromones and that new approaches are needed to demonstrate them.[6]

A frequently cited objection is that the genes for vomeronasal receptors are nonfunctional pseudogenes in humans and the organ appears to regress in adults, so a mechanism for detecting pheromones is uncertain. Jacob (2005) is cited as a skeptical review.[1][2] Proponents point to trace amine-associated receptors in the nasal lining as a possible detector, and to a 2019 report that a putative pheromone affected men's sexual cognition.[2]
The statement that no human pheromone has been demonstrated is itself listed as disputed, and the overall status of human pheromones is described as speculative and controversial.[2]

No studies found testing androstadienone or copulins as agents for increasing attractiveness in real-world dating or mating. Laboratory studies of androstadienone and mood, attention and cortisol are described above.[1]

Some body spray advertisers state that their products contain human sexual pheromones that act as aphrodisiacs. The cited reviews say such marketing goes beyond what peer-reviewed studies have shown, and Wikipedia notes that the androstadienone article's own account is limited to small laboratory effects on mood and attention.[1][2]

Pheromone fragrances belong to a wider category of scent products used to change how a person is perceived. Companies selling them typically present androstadienone or similar steroids as a hidden attractant, and the compound is also the main ingredient in laboratory use of the term human sex pheromone, a label that the 2025 review in Physiology & Behavior called inconclusive.[1][5]

On T Nation, threads titled 'Does Your Sweat Turn Women On?' and 'The Gym's Aphrodisiac' repost articles summarizing a study in which women smelled swabs of androstadienone, a constituent of sweat, and a placebo, with physiological measures taken; the posts present it as evidence that men's sweat can affect women's arousal.[12][13]

Related claims about body odor and attraction include the McClintock effect on menstrual synchrony, preferences for the scent of people whose immune (MHC) genes differ from one's own proposed by Milinski and Wedekind, and the idea that women find androstenone more pleasant around ovulation.[2] Wikipedia describes the role of pheromones in human behavior overall as speculative and controversial.[2]

lore.intro: Pheromone claims appear in fitness and attraction forums mainly as reposted articles about sweat chemistry and as the premise of pheromone colognes.[12][13]

claims.claim: Men's sweat contains a chemical that affects women's arousal and mood.
claims.believers: T Nation posts cite a study in which women smelled androstadienone and a placebo and had body temperature, skin conductance, pulse and other measures recorded.[12][13]
claims.experts: Laboratory studies report mood, attention and cortisol effects in women, while reviews state that the pheromone classification is inconclusive and that many positive findings may be false positives.[1][5][6]

claims.claim: Cologne additives containing androstadienone make the wearer more attractive.
claims.believers: Advertisers state that their products contain human sexual pheromones that act as aphrodisiacs.[2]
claims.experts: Wikipedia states that no pheromonal substance has been shown in a peer-reviewed study to directly change human behavior, and its androstadienone article notes small mood and attention effects only in laboratory settings.[1][2]

claims.claim: Androstadienone shifts women's preferences toward more masculine faces.
claims.believers: A 2020 randomized trial reported a rightward shift in preference for sexually dimorphic male faces after exposure.[8]
claims.experts: A 2024 pre-registered study found little evidence for a related prosocial effect, and reviews highlight small samples and reproducibility concerns.[9][6]

claims.claim: Humans have a working pheromone-detection system like animals do.
claims.believers: Proponents point to trace amine-associated receptors in the nose as a possible detector, and to brain-imaging studies reporting hypothalamic responses to androstadienone.[2][21]
claims.experts: Reviews note that the vomeronasal organ's receptor genes are nonfunctional in adults and that physiological levels of androstadienone in sweat appear too low to act alone.[2][14][16]

claims.claim: Androstadienone works on women only when they are attracted to men.
claims.believers: Studies reporting sex- and orientation-dependent brain and mood responses are cited as showing the compound acts as a sex-specific signal.[15][17]
claims.experts: Reviews report that effects depend on context, such as the experimenter's sex, and differ between individuals; a 2025 review calls the pheromone classification inconclusive.[15][16][5]

claims.claim: Published positive results show human pheromones are real.
claims.believers: Almost 60 studies have reported significant results for androstadienone and estratetraenol.[6]
claims.experts: The authors of the 2020 Royal Society B review say these may be false positives from small samples and call for pre-registration, while adding that humans may still have pheromones.[6]

card.summary: The idea that sweat steroids and vaginal acids work as human attraction chemicals; lab effects on mood are reported, behavior change is unshown.
card.note: Reviews say no pheromone has been shown to directly change human behavior; product marketing goes beyond the research.

quick.overview:
Androstadienone is a steroid in male sweat and semen, and copulins are fatty acids in vaginal fluid. Both have been proposed as human pheromones, and androstadienone is sold as an additive in colognes marketed to increase attraction.

Lab studies have reported small changes in women's mood, attention and cortisol after smelling androstadienone. Reviews say that no pheromone has been shown to directly change human behavior, and researchers dispute this.
quick.mechanism: In animals, pheromones act through the vomeronasal organ. In humans the organ's receptor genes are nonfunctional, so proponents point to other nasal receptors as a possible route, which remains unconfirmed.
quick.risks: No specific harms are documented for the compounds in fragrance use. The main caveat in the literature is that product marketing claims go beyond the published evidence.

chain: Androstadienone or pheromone-style additive worn in a fragrance
Greater attraction toward the wearer, according to marketing
angle.text: Pheromone colognes and sprays are marketed on the idea that androstadienone makes the wearer more attractive. Laboratory studies have measured mood, attention and preference shifts in women, not real-world attraction.[1][5]
